replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
So decompile it self was accessible from early times, however actually getting back useful source code is harder and it depends really on language.

If you want recreate the game decompile is not enough you actually need to have proper naming for functions variables etc. That is less hard with Java and C#, because they store metadata for types, but for C++ it is way harder(if it is unreal engine it maybe simpler, because you know what code to expect). The reason is why it is harder, because the code becomes assembly with tons of inlining and optimisation. I did not see yet that happening with complex commercial games.

People throwing around decompile word with the pass through mods, but most of them is just made by using simple mods.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: I have some doubts. for example, if you decompile a unity game, you may end up dealing with PhyX (unity's prosperity built-in physics engine). no idea how deep the rabbit hole is... well I suppose that's AI's headache

comments.author: ThreeDMK
comments.body: I have burned 2 full Claude Max 20x weeks building tooling to datamine the World of Warcraft game client.  Now I have scripts that can pull data from each build when it drops (retail, tbc, beta, classic).  At this point I feel like nothing is safe or protected anymore so I just build accordingly.

comments.author: BrianScottGregory
comments.body: If you can successfully decompile a game into source code that is then compilable and it actually works like the original compiled game, then yes, you can absolutely make changes to physics - or whatever else you want, since you now have access to the source code.
